en: The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Questions of the Virtuous Daughter, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of South India during the Tang Dynasty by imperial decree.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Abode of the Rishis in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
In the Deer Park, he was accompanied by a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus and an immeasurable multitude of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

At that time, at the hour of the meal, the World-Honored One donned his robes, took up his bowl, and together with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Ajita, entered the great city of Vārāṇasī to beg for food. Proceeding through the city in succession to collect alms, he arrived at the home of the virtuous brahmin woman.

At that time, the virtuous woman saw from afar that the Tathāgata’s physical form was majestic and dignified, his faculties were tranquil, and his mind was serene, vast, and unsurpassed. His deportment and glances were deliberate, composed, and refined, like a dragon king of great majesty and virtue; he was as firm and stable as a pillar of pure gold, as clear and free from turbidity as a pristine pool, and as unmoved by joy or sorrow as one in the fourth dhyāna. From his body emanated a radiance that penetrated both internally and externally with perfect clarity.

At that time, the virtuous woman, seeing such signs, conceived pure faith in her heart. She approached the Buddha, prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ajita, and with a bowed body and respectful demeanor, joined her palms toward the Buddha and spoke these words: "Welcome! "
World-Honored One! Welcome!
Well-Gone One!
"I now wish to inquire about my doubts; I only pray that you will deign to show compassion and remain here for a short while.
At that time, the World-Honored One silently accepted the request, spread his seat, and sat down, and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ajita also sat down following the Buddha.
At that time, the Brahmin woman Guṇavatī felt great joy and, increasing her reverence even further, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I have heard that the Tathāgata turned the wondrous Wheel of Dharma at the Deer Park in the Abode of the Sages at Vārāṇasī; yet I do not yet know what kind of Dharma the World-Honored One has taught by turning this Wheel of Dharma.”
The Buddha said to her: "Virtuous lady! I turn the wheel of Dharma, declaring that ignorance conditions volitional formations;

volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions existence; existence conditions birth; and birth conditions old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair."

With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; and with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair cease.
"O virtuous daughter!

This is the wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgata at the Abode of the Sages in the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī; among all those in the world—whether śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, māras, or brahmās—none are able to turn it in accordance with the Dharma."
At that time, the Brahmin woman Guṇavatī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what is called ignorance, does it exist internally?”
"Is it because there is something external? The Buddha said, "No."
The virtuous woman said:
“World-Honored One!
If there is no ignorance within or without, how could there be formations conditioned by ignorance?”
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
are there dharmas from other worlds that come to this present world?
The Buddha said:
"No," the virtuous woman replied again to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One!"
"Is the characteristic of ignorance substantially existent? The Buddha said, "No."
"The intrinsic nature of ignorance arises from false conceptualization; it does not arise from reality. It arises from perversion; it does not arise from accordance with reality.
The virtuous woman then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
If it were thus, there would be no ignorance; how then could the arising of volitional formations occur, leading to the experience of various bitter retributions within birth and death?
World-Honored One!

Just as a tree that lacks roots cannot have branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, or other such things, so too, because ignorance has no intrinsic nature, the arising of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and the subsequent links is certainly impossible.
The Buddha said, “O virtuous woman! All dharmas are ultimately empty.

Yet the foolish and deluded do not hear the meaning of emptiness; even if they were to hear it, they lack the wisdom to understand it. Consequently, they fully create all manner of karmas. Once there are these various karmas, the various realms of existence arise, and within those realms, one undergoes all manner of suffering.”
"In the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there are no karmic actions, nor are there any states of existence born from karma, nor any various matters of suffering and affliction.
O Virtuous Woman!"

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, in accordance with the world, extensively expounds all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings, desiring to cause them to realize and understand the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
O virtuous daughter!
Even the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is established by following worldly convention and given a name. Why is this so?
Within the ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*), both the subject that perceives and the object perceived are entirely unfindable.
"O Virtuous Daughter!

It is like when the Buddhas manifest emanated beings, and these emanated beings further manifest various other things; those emanated beings are deceptive and unreal, and the things they manifest likewise lack any substantial reality."
“This too is likewise: the various karmas that are created are deceptive and unreal; birth arising from karma likewise has no substantial reality.
At that time, the lady Guṇavati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, the wheel of Dharma turned by the Tathāgata now is the wheel of space, the wheel of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the wheel of transcendence, the wheel of penetration, the wheel of the inconceivable, the wheel that no one can turn, the wheel without equal, the wheel of reality as it is, the wheel of non-arising, the wheel of the absence of intrinsic nature, and the wheel of signlessness.
“World-Honored One!
Thus has the Wheel of Dharma been turned by the Tathāgata.
Having spoken these words, he immediately took powdered candana sandalwood in both hands, scattered it over the Buddha’s feet, and said:
“World-Honored One!
By the power of these roots of goodness, may I, in a future age, be able to turn such various wheels of Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One smiled serenely and emitted various rays of light from his mouth. These rays were brilliant and radiant, encompassing all colors, and reached throughout immeasurable worlds in the ten directions, filling every single world without exception. They then returned to the Buddha’s presence, circled him three times to the right, and entered through the crown of the Buddha’s head.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ajita addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
for what cause and condition does the Tathāgata now suddenly smile?”
"As I understand it, this is not without causes and conditions. The Buddha said to him, "Ajita!"
"Do you see this brahmin woman, who is holding powdered sandalwood in her hands and scattering it over my feet?
He replied, "I have seen her."

The Buddha said: “By virtue of the roots of goodness planted now, this girl shall not fall into the evil realms for eighty-four thousand *koṭis* of *kalpas*. She will serve and make offerings with a heart of deep respect to sixty-four thousand Buddhas, hearing, protecting, and upholding the True Dharma.

Throughout the time those Buddhas remain in the world and after their parinirvāṇa, she will continue this practice without interruption. Furthermore, she will cause immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings to turn toward Bodhi. Thereafter, within this trichiliocosm, during the eon called Prabhāsa, she will attain Buddhahood under the name Dharmaprabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. That Buddha’s lifespan will last for a full *kalpa*, and he will teach and transform immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings, leading them to attain nirvāṇa.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ajita again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What roots of goodness did this virtuous Brahmin woman plant in past lives?”
The Buddha said, “Ajita!

You should know now that in a past age, when the Buddha Vipaśyin appeared in the world, this virtuous woman was already in the female form. Seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, she untied the necklaces she was wearing upon her body and offered them to that Buddha as an act of worship.”

"When the Tathāgata Śikhin appeared in the world, I questioned him regarding profound meanings at his dwelling and made offerings of exquisite robes. Within that Dharma, I left the household life to study the Path and practiced the holy life (brahmacarya) for a full thousand years."

"When the Buddha Vipaśyin appeared in the world, I prepared various kinds of excellent food and drink, making offerings to that Buddha and his assembly of śrāvakas for half a month; whatever they required according to their wishes was provided without deficiency."
"When the Buddha Krakucchanda appeared in the world, I scattered atimuktaka flowers over that Buddha as an offering and received the five precepts, upholding them without deficiency."

"When the Buddha Kanakamuni appeared in the world, I vowed to provide him with various kinds of food, drink, clothing, bedding, medicinal requisites, and all other necessities for his person, making offerings throughout the entirety of his lifespan. At that time, for two months, that Buddha accepted from me offerings of food, drink, leather sandals, and other articles for his personal use."
"When the Tathāgata Kāśyapa appeared in the world, I again scattered golden flowers as an offering to the Buddha; all such deeds were performed for the sake of seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
She further made this vow:
"By these roots of goodness from my offerings, may I swiftly receive the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; if I do not receive that prediction, I shall never again relinquish this female body."
"Ānanda! Such were the roots of goodness planted by this virtuous Brahmin woman in her past lives; this is her final retribution for being born as a woman."

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ajita, the virtuous Brahmin woman, and all those in the world—gods, humans, asuras, and others—were filled with great joy; they believed, accepted, and practiced it.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Questions of the Virtuous Woman (Guṇavara-dārikā-paripṛcchā)
